extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, and readers interested in scientific publishing ethics and policy
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and assess criteria used to judge the quality, integrity, and impact of scientific journals and their editorial/publishing practices (retractions, peer review, conflicts, metrics). Useful for analyzing journals' behavior and policy debates about publication incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction Index
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculates the rate of retraction per 1,000 papers published (Fang & Casadevall’s Retraction Index).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to compare journals' retraction rates (table shows Science 1.754, Nature 1.296, Cell 3.794, PNAS 1.064 for 2006–2011). The post uses the Retraction Index to argue PNAS had a lower index than the other glamour journals, but notes absolute and contextual factors matter (e.g., PNAS's 23 retractions vs 28 for Cell/Nature/Science combined).

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact Factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal impact factor as a commonly cited metric of journal 'importance' (numbers provided alongside retraction data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impact factor appears in the comparison (Science 32.452, Nature 36.235, Cell 34.774, PNAS 10.472). The post questions use of impact factor as a proxy for quality and notes Fang & Casadevall's observed correlation between impact factor and retraction index.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute number of retractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Total count of retracted papers in a journal over a given period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article reports absolute counts (e.g., PNAS 23 retractions 2006–2011; Cell/Nature/Science together 28) and points out that many retractions occur outside the highest-profile journals (1,300 in other journals), so absolute counts must be interpreted in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of retraction and correction
rubrics_metrics.description: How quickly a journal retracts flawed or fraudulent work, or issues corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: a cheetah fossil retraction took four years (three during Schekman’s tenure); an exchange where concerns raised in 2006 only led to retraction two years later, during which the paper accrued ten citations. Delays are presented as causing additional harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to publish critiques, letters, and replication attempts
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a journal publishes letters of critique and replication studies following contested papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PNAS reportedly would not publish a letter of critique in the cheetah fossil case, while Science published multiple letters and two replication attempts in the arsenic life controversy. Openness to critique and replication is framed as an important corrective mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial responsiveness and investigative process
rubrics_metrics.description: How editors and editorial boards handle complaints, engage with critics, and decide on further action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Diener’s experience: managing editor communicated authors’ reply and the Editorial Board concluded 'no additional action is required' despite ongoing concerns; later the paper was retracted. The process, communications, and intermediate decisions are important evaluation points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest and editorial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether editors, funders, or institutional relationships create conflicts that influence review and publication decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerns raised about HHMI/Wellcome Trust funding eLife (possible pressure to review or favor HHMI-funded research) and about PNAS ‘contributed’ articles where editors/authors may be reviewed by friends or former students. Such conflicts are flagged as undermining fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on junior researchers and career consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: How editorial policies or personal boycotts affect junior lab members’ careers and opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schekman’s pledge to boycott Cell/Nature/Science is noted as potentially punishing his junior researchers, who rely on publications in high-profile journals for careers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication bias and risk-tolerance for novel claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The tendency of high-impact journals to publish riskier, more sensational claims quickly, accepting greater chance of later retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post characterizes glamour journals as ‘willing to publish riskier, but potentially higher-impact claims ASAP’ and suggests more retractions are a likely price for getting high-impact science out early. This is framed as both a virtue (speed) and a vice (integrity risk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using journal metrics to judge individuals (venue-based evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessing researchers by where they publish (journal brand/impact factor) rather than by the intrinsic quality of their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schekman urges funders and universities not to judge papers by where they are published — 'the quality of the science, not the journal’s brand, that matters.' The post and commenters discuss how hiring/tenure/funding committees often rely on venue-based shortcuts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections and detection of inappropriate data use
rubrics_metrics.description: Tracking corrections where data were misused (e.g., same data used across different experiments) and other non-retraction corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commenter suggests adding a 'corrections' column to datasets to capture inappropriate data reuse and self-plagiarism; the post acknowledges corrections are an important complement to retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citations of retracted papers as a harm metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Measuring the damage of flawed papers by how many citations they accrued prior to retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commenter suggests that citations-of-retracted-papers may be a better metric of harm than raw retraction counts — e.g., many quick retractions with no citations do little damage, whereas a long-delayed retraction after many citations causes large downstream harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of editorial communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether editorial correspondence, decision rationales, and author responses are made public or at least made available to complainants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the Diener case editors included the authors’ reply and encouraged contact, but did not publish a critique — raising questions about how transparent and accountable editorial communications are.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial board composition and nepotism
rubrics_metrics.description: Overlap between editorial boards and authorship that may produce favoritism or elite-club dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters worry elite journals and subsidiary journals may share names on editorial boards and authorship, potentially creating closed networks that favor insiders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review model effectiveness (double-blind vs open)
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of peer review model and its ability to reduce bias or fail in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-blind review is proposed as a way to reduce bias and force careful reading, but commenters note anonymity often fails (self-citations reveal identity) and that eLife missed an opportunity not to adopt double-blind review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher ownership and profit motives
rubrics_metrics.description: The influence of for-profit publishers and corporate interests on what is published and how integrity is enforced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters argue corporate control and profit motives can suppress unfavorable research and prioritize metrics like impact factor over scientific integrity; this is raised as a structural concern about publishing incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness of submission pathways (contributed articles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether special submission routes (e.g., 'contributed' by editors) give some authors different review options and create unfair advantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism of PNAS’s contributed-by mechanism where editors might be last authors and papers are reviewed by friends/former trainees is highlighted as an anti-pattern that undermines fair peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systemic accountability and enforcement options
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals for stronger enforcement against fraud (e.g., criminal penalties, repayment of grant monies) as part of the ecosystem for maintaining integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commenter suggests making science-fraud-linked grant awards a criminal offense and repaying monies as a deterrent; the post includes this as an example of thinking about remedies beyond editorial correction.
